92.title: Migration to Abyssinia
92.hook: a band of persecuted believers flee across the sea to a just Christian king, and Ja'far recites Surah Maryam before him
92.howItsDone: Muslims remember the migration to Abyssinia as the first hijra and honor the Negus as a just ruler; the story is often told as an early example of friendship between Muslims and Christians.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bilal on the burning sand. Your line was ahad, ahad: One, One.

Beaten, starved, locked up: that's Mecca now for believers with no powerful family to protect them. And the Prophet ﷺ tells some of them: go. Cross the sea to Abyssinia, in East Africa. There's a king there, he says, under whom no one is wronged. So small groups slip down to the coast, onto boats, across the Red Sea. Refugees, families with children, among them his own daughter Ruqayyah, and his cousin Ja'far, 'Ali's brother. In a Christian kingdom, they can pray in peace. Then a delegation from Mecca arrives, carrying expensive gifts for the king.
screen: `NO ONE TO PROTECT THEM.` → `A KING UNDER WHOM NO ONE IS WRONGED.` → `REFUGEES ACROSS THE RED SEA.`

segments.voice: The delegation asks the king, the Najashi, the Negus, to hand the refugees back. He says: I won't hand over people who came to me for shelter until I've heard them. The account, told by Umm Salamah, who was there, is preserved in Ibn Ishaq and in the Musnad of Ahmad. The Muslims choose Ja'far to speak. We were a people in ignorance, he says, worshiping idols, cutting family ties, the strong eating up the weak. Then Allah sent us a messenger from among us, whose honesty we knew, and he told us to worship One God, to speak the truth, keep trusts, be good to our relatives and neighbors, and stop harming one another. The king asks: do you have anything of what he brought? Ja'far recites from the opening of Surah Maryam. After its opening letters, in Pickthall's words: “A mention of the mercy of thy Lord unto His servant Zachariah.” It's the surah of nida'an khafiyya, of Maryam, an-nakhlah and the baby in the cradle, from week eleven of this path. The account says the king wept until his beard was wet, and the bishops around him wept too. And he said: this, and what Isa brought, come from the same source of light. Go in peace; I won't give you up. The delegation went home with their gifts. The Muslims stayed for years. When the Negus died, the Prophet ﷺ led a funeral prayer for him in Medina, far away, as a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari reports. Muslims remember him with deep gratitude: a Christian king who protected strangers because it was just.
screen: `HAND THEM BACK, SAYS MECCA.` · `JA'FAR: WHO WE WERE, WHO WE ARE.` · `SURAH MARYAM, AND THE KING WEEPS.` · `I WILL NOT GIVE YOU UP.` · then, large: `A JUST KING.`

segments.voice: Think of someone near you who is new, or far from home: a family who just moved in, a colleague still learning the language, a student from another country. Picture where they sit and who doesn't talk to them, then one small way to make room: a greeting by name, an invitation, a question about where they're from, and real listening to the answer. If you pray, you can ask Allah to protect them.
Najashi. The Christian king of Abyssinia who sheltered the persecuted believers and refused to hand them back.
Your line: a just king. Tomorrow, a year of two great losses. That's day ninety-two.

93.title: The year of sorrow
93.hook: in one year, he loses both Khadijah and Abu Talib, his wife and his protector
93.carry: grief is a year, not a day
93.howItsDone: Muslims say inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un on hearing of any death or loss; mourning is marked with prayer, visits and food for the bereaved, and tears are understood as mercy, not weakness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Najashi, the king who wept at Surah Maryam. Your line was a just king.

Some years take more than one thing from you. The same year the job goes, the parent gets sick. The second loss doesn't just add to the first; it lands on a bruise. For the Prophet ﷺ, some years after the cave, came a year like that. The Muslims had just come through a long boycott, years when Quraysh refused to trade with his whole clan or marry into it, and families went hungry in a narrow valley. It had finally ended. Then, within a short time of each other, the two people who had held him up all his life died.
screen: `SOME YEARS TAKE TWO THINGS.` → `A LONG BOYCOTT, JUST ENDED.` → `THEN, TWO DEATHS.`

segments.voice: First his uncle, Abu Talib, who took him in at eight, raised him, and through years of mounting hostility stood between his nephew and Quraysh, because in that society an attack on him meant answering to his clan. Muslims differ on Abu Talib's faith: Sunni scholars follow a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari that says he died without accepting Islam, while Shi'a Muslims hold that he was a believer. Both remember his protection with honor. Then Khadijah, his wife, who saw him first, who wrapped him in a blanket and said, Allah would never disgrace you. Muslims call it 'am al-huzn, the Year of Sorrow. It didn't end there. With Abu Talib gone, the protection went too, and the insults grew bolder. Ibn Ishaq tells how someone threw dirt on the Prophet's head in the street, and at home one of his daughters washed it off, crying, and he told her: don't cry, my daughter, Allah will protect your father. Nobody is told to hurry past this; the seerah names a whole year after grief. Years later, when the Prophet's baby son Ibrahim died, a hadith in Bukhari says he wept openly and said: the eyes shed tears and the heart grieves, and we say only what pleases our Lord. There, tears and faith sit side by side. The Qur'an gives words for moments like this, words Muslims say on hearing of a death: “Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning.” And another surah: “But lo! with hardship goeth ease.”
screen: `ABU TALIB, HIS PROTECTOR.` · `KHADIJAH, WHO SAW HIM FIRST.` · `'AM AL-HUZN: A YEAR NAMED FOR GRIEF.` · `THE EYES SHED TEARS; THE HEART GRIEVES.` · then, large: `GRIEF IS A YEAR, NOT A DAY.`

segments.voice: If you've had a season when more than one thing went at once, let it come to mind gently, without reliving it: name both things quietly, and let it be as heavy as it is. If you haven't had a year like that, think of someone who is in one now. If you pray, you can say: inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un, we belong to Allah, and to Him we return.
'Am al-huzn, the Year of Sorrow: when he lost both Khadijah and Abu Talib, his wife and his protector.
Your line: grief is a year, not a day. Tomorrow, he looks for help in another town. Day ninety-three.

94.title: The road from Ta'if
94.hook: stoned out of Ta'if and bleeding, he is offered revenge, and refuses it
94.tomorrow: the Night Journey and the Hijra
94.howItsDone: Muslims tell the story of Ta'if as a picture of the Prophet's mercy toward those who hurt him, and it is recalled when Muslims are tempted to answer cruelty with revenge.

segments.voice: Yesterday, 'am al-huzn, the year of sorrow. Your line was grief is a year, not a day.
screen: `GRIEF IS A YEAR, NOT A DAY.`

segments.voice: With his protector gone, Mecca is closing in, so the Prophet ﷺ walks up into the mountains to Ta'if, a cooler, greener town; later accounts say Zayd, the freed slave he raised as a son, walks with him. He asks its leaders: will you listen? Will you give me shelter? They don't just say no. They mock him. As he leaves, Ibn Ishaq says, they stir up the town's slaves and louts to shout after him. Later accounts add the stones: Zayd trying to shield him, and the Prophet's feet bleeding until his sandals were soaked.
screen: `A WALK TO TA'IF.` → `THEY MOCK HIM.` → `STONES, AND BLEEDING FEET.`

segments.voice: Years later, 'Aishah asked whether any day had been harder than the battle of Uhud. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari gives his answer: the hardest was the day he went to a leader of Ta'if and was turned away. He walked on, dazed, not knowing where he was, until he looked up and saw a cloud shading him. In it was Jibril: Allah has heard what your people said to you. With him, the angel of the mountains: if you wish, I will bring the two mountains together and crush them. Bleeding, humiliated, with no one left to protect him, he's offered what a hurt person might want most: justice, revenge. The Prophet said no. Then this: I hope that Allah will bring out from their children people who will worship Allah alone. Not them. Their children. On the way home, Ibn Ishaq says, he rests in a garden, bleeding, and a servant named 'Addas brings him grapes. He says bismillah and eats. 'Addas is surprised: people here don't say that. Where are you from? Nineveh. And the Prophet answers: the town of the good man Yunus, son of Matta. He was my brother; he was a prophet, and I am a prophet. Yunus, from day seventy-five. Turned away by a town himself, the Prophet calls a prophet from Nineveh his brother. The hope came true: years later, Ibn Ishaq says, Thaqif, the tribe of Ta'if, sent a delegation and accepted Islam. The Qur'an says to the Prophet, in Pickthall's words: “We sent thee not save as a mercy for the peoples.”
screen: `HARDER THAN UHUD.` · `THE ANGEL OF THE MOUNTAINS.` · `GRAPES, AND A MAN FROM NINEVEH.` · `THE HOPE CAME TRUE.` · then, large: `NOT THEM, THEIR CHILDREN.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who hurt you, someone manageable, not the worst in your life; if part of you would like them to suffer a little, just notice it. Then, if you can, widen the frame to their children, the people who come after them. If you pray, you can ask Allah to guide them, or to bring good from what comes after them; if you don't, just wish their children well.
Ta'if, the town where he was stoned and offered revenge, and instead hoped for their children.
Your line: not them, their children. Tomorrow, a night journey, and the road out of Mecca. See you then.

95.title: The Night Journey and the Hijra
95.hook: after the night journey and the pledges at 'Aqabah, he slips out of Mecca, hides in a cave, and tells Abu Bakr: do not grieve, Allah is with us
95.howItsDone: Some communities mark the Isra and Mi'raj on the 27th of Rajab, and the Islamic calendar counts its years from the Hijra.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ta'if. Your line was not them, their children.

After Ta'if, a night. Surah seventeen opens with it, in Pickthall's words: “Glorified be He Who carried His servant by night from the Inviolable Place of Worship to the Far Distant Place of Worship.” Muslims understand the Far Distant Place as Jerusalem; that night journey is the Isra. Then, they say, came the ascent through the heavens, the Mi'raj, where, a hadith in Bukhari says, the five daily prayers were given. Some early voices held it was a journey of the spirit; others, of body and soul. After the year of sorrow, it is told as an honor and a comfort. At the pilgrimage season, men from Yathrib meet him at night at 'Aqabah and pledge to protect him as they would their own families.
screen: `THE NIGHT JOURNEY.` → `THE FIVE PRAYERS GIVEN.` → `A PLEDGE AT 'AQABAH.`

segments.voice: So the Muslims of Mecca begin leaving for Yathrib, quietly, a few at a time, leaving houses and businesses behind. Quraysh's leaders decide: before he can go, kill him. One young man from each clan, so the blame is shared and his family can't take revenge on anyone. The Qur'an mentions their plotting. That night, the Prophet ﷺ asks 'Ali to sleep in his bed, under his green cloak, and slips out with Abu Bakr. Instead of heading north toward Yathrib, where everyone would look, they go south, up to a cave on Mount Thawr, and hide there three nights. Abu Bakr's daughter Asma' brings food, tearing her waistband in two to tie up the bundles. The trackers come right up to the mouth of the cave. Abu Bakr whispers: if one of them looks down at his feet, he'll see us. The Prophet answers, in Sahih al-Bukhari: what do you think of two, when Allah is the third? Surah At-Tawbah remembers him as “the second of two; when they two were in the cave, when he said unto his comrade: Grieve not. Lo! Allah is with us.” People also tell of a spider that spun a web across the cave's mouth, and a dove that nested there, so the trackers thought the cave empty; the Qur'an doesn't mention it, and scholars differ on how reliable the report is. The trackers leave, and the two set out for Yathrib. This leaving is the hijra: the migration, the breaking away. A hadith in Bukhari widens the word: the true emigrant is the one who leaves behind what Allah forbids.
screen: `ONE MAN FROM EACH CLAN.` · `'ALI SLEEPS IN HIS BED.` · `THREE NIGHTS IN THE CAVE OF THAWR.` · `WHAT OF TWO, WHEN ALLAH IS THIRD?` · then, large: `GRIEVE NOT. LO! ALLAH IS WITH US.`

segments.voice: Make a small cave: a closet, a car, or just your hands cupped over your eyes. Let one fear come to the entrance, and whisper, so quietly only you can hear: if you pray, Allah is with us; if you don't, I'm not alone in here.
Hijra. The migration: the Prophet's leaving of Mecca for Yathrib, breaking with the old to begin again.
Your line: Allah is with us. Tomorrow, the last day of the stories. Day ninety-five, done.

96.title: Camp 2 close: the camel kneels
96.hook: he reaches Yathrib, where his camel kneels on a plot of land, a mosque is built, and the calendar begins again
96.howItsDone: Muslims date the Islamic year from the Hijra, and many visit the Prophet's Mosque in Medina, which stands on the land where his camel knelt; the first of Muharram marks the Islamic new year.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the cave of Thawr. Your line was Allah is with us. Today, the last day of the stories.

For days, Yathrib has walked out to the edge of town every morning, watching the road from Mecca in the heat, and gone home disappointed. Then one day a lookout shouts: he's here. The whole town pours out. First he stops at Quba, just outside, and builds a simple mosque there, the first in Islam. In town, everyone wants him. Clan after clan grabs his camel's reins: stay with us. And he says, gently: let her go. She is under orders. The camel, al-Qaswa', walks on through the streets, the whole town following, holding its breath.
screen: `EVERY MORNING, WATCHING THE ROAD.` → `QUBA: THE FIRST MOSQUE.` → `LET HER GO. SHE IS UNDER ORDERS.`

segments.voice: Ibn Ishaq and Sahih al-Bukhari both tell where she knelt: an open yard where dates were laid out to dry, which belonged to two orphan boys. They offered it as a gift; he insisted on paying. There, carrying bricks with his own hands alongside everyone else, he built the mosque that, rebuilt and enlarged many times, still stands at the heart of the city. Yathrib got a new name: Madinat an-Nabi, the city of the Prophet, or simply al-Madinah, the city. Those who came from Mecca were the muhajirun, the emigrants; those of Medina who took them in, the ansar, the helpers. Years later, the Muslims began counting their calendar from this year, six hundred and twenty-two. Not from his birth, not from the cave. From the hijra, the year a community began. That's where the stories end, for now. Seventy-four days ago, on day twenty-two, you met Adam, the steward the angels questioned. Then Iblis who would not bow, and the garden with its one tree. Two sons. Nuh building on dry land. Ibrahim and the idols, the fire made cool, Hajar running between the hills, the House raised. Musa in a basket on the river, the fire on the mountain, the sea. Yusuf, from the well to forgive one old thing, out loud. Maryam, Zakariyya and Yahya, Isa by Allah's leave. Yunus in three darknesses. And then the Prophet ﷺ himself: an orphan in the desert, a trusted young man, a cave, one word, read, and a road out of Mecca. You know these stories now.

97.title: The intention
97.hook: every prayer begins in the heart, not on the tongue
97.howItsDone: Before each prayer, fast or act of worship, Muslims form an intention in the heart, naming to themselves which prayer or deed it is and that it is for Allah; scholars differ on whether also saying it quietly is recommended.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the camel knelt in Medina, and camp two closed with seventy-five days of stories, counting from the hijra. Your line was you know these stories now. Today, camp three: the practices.

Two people drop a twenty in the same charity box. One does it because someone important is watching. The other, because of a child she saw in the news this morning. From the outside, nothing tells them apart: same twenty, same box. For the next stretch, this path turns from stories to practices, the things Muslims actually do, starting with the prayer, salat, step by step. And the first step of the prayer isn't a movement or a word. It happens where no one can see it.
screen: `TWO PEOPLE, ONE TWENTY, ONE BOX.` → `FROM STORIES TO PRACTICES.` → `THE FIRST STEP IS INVISIBLE.`

segments.voice: The word is niyyah: intention, what you mean by what you're about to do. Sahih al-Bukhari opens with a hadith about it. The Prophet ﷺ said, in its meaning: actions are only by their intentions, and each person gets only what they intended. Then he gives an example. Two people make the same journey, the hijra you just followed to Medina. One goes for Allah and His messenger. The other goes for something of this world, or to marry someone. Same road, same dust, different journeys. So before every prayer, a Muslim forms the intention: this is the noon prayer, four units, for Allah. Where does that happen? The scholars place it in the heart. You don't have to say it out loud; if your heart knows what it's doing, the niyyah is there. Some, especially in the Shafi'i school, recommend saying it quietly as well, to help the heart focus. Either way, it isn't a formula. It's a turning. A hadith in Sahih Muslim says Allah does not look at your bodies or your faces, but at your hearts and your deeds. And one in Bukhari is tender: if someone intends a good deed and then can't do it, it is still written for them as a good deed. The intention itself counts. In that reading, an ordinary day can become worship when it's meant. The Qur'an gives words for that: “Lo! my worship and my sacrifice and my living and my dying are for Allah, Lord of the Worlds.” Living, too, not just praying.
screen: `NIYYAH: WHAT YOU MEAN BY IT.` · `ACTIONS ARE BY INTENTIONS.` · `IN THE HEART, NOT ON THE TONGUE.` · `A GOOD INTENTION IS WRITTEN.` · then, large: `MEAN IT FIRST.`

segments.voice: Before the sit begins, ask yourself one quiet question: why am I doing this? Not the right answer, the real one: to feel calmer, to learn, to be close to Allah, because someone I love prays. Let the answer be honest, then begin on purpose; if you pray, you can make your intention for Allah.

98.title: Clean body, clean place
98.hook: wudu, clean clothes, a clean spot, and the idea behind them
98.howItsDone: Before each prayer, Muslims make sure they are in wudu (the ritual washing of face, arms, head and feet), that their clothes are clean, and that they pray on a clean spot, often a prayer rug; with no water, they use tayammum with clean earth.

segments.voice: Yesterday: niyyah, the intention, formed in the heart. Your line was mean it first. Behind us now: a small band crossing the sea to a just king, a year of grief, a bloody road out of Ta'if, a night journey, a migration, a camel kneeling in Medina.

A man rolls up his sleeves at work, in the restroom, and washes his hands, his mouth, his face, his arms to the elbow, wipes his head, washes his feet. A coworker walks in and looks a little puzzled. He's not being fussy. He's getting ready. Before anyone says a word of the prayer, the cleanness comes first.
screen: `A SINK AT WORK.` → `A COWORKER LOOKS PUZZLED.` → `HE'S GETTING READY.`

segments.voice: The Arabic word is taharah, purity or cleanness. Books of Islamic law put it ahead of the chapter on prayer, because the prayer isn't valid without it. It has three layers. First, the body. For the daily prayers that usually means wudu, the washing the Qur'an itself describes in Surah al-Ma'idah: wash your faces, and your hands up to the elbows, wipe your heads, and wash your feet up to the ankles. After some things, like sleep or using the toilet, wudu needs renewing. After others, like sex, a full bath is needed, called ghusl. Second, the clothes: clean of things like urine or blood. Third, the place: a clean spot to stand on. That's what a prayer rug is for. It isn't holy in itself, just a clean surface you can carry anywhere. Here's the surprise. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said, in a hadith in Bukhari, that the whole earth had been made for him a place of prayer and a means of purification. A field, a parking lot, the edge of an airport gate: any clean ground will do. When there's no water, or water would harm you, there's tayammum: you touch clean earth or dust and wipe your face and hands. The idea behind it all is in a short hadith in Sahih Muslim: purity is half of faith. Not a rule tacked on to the prayer. Half of the thing itself. Some scholars read it as outside and inside together: the water on the skin, and the turning of the heart it's meant to go with.
screen: `TAHARAH — BEFORE EVERYTHING ELSE.` · `THE BODY, THE CLOTHES, THE PLACE.` · `THE WHOLE EARTH, A PLACE OF PRAYER.` · `PURITY IS HALF OF FAITH.` · then, large: `OUTSIDE AND INSIDE TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Clear one small spot near you, a corner of the floor, a chair, a patch of desk, and if you have a clean cloth, a towel or a scarf, lay it down flat and smooth it with your hands. Sit near it, breathing slowly, and look: a small place where nothing is piled up. If you've done wudu before, notice where the water would go; if you pray, this is the kind of place you'd pray on.
Taharah. Cleanness of body, clothes and place, the half of faith that comes before the prayer. Today's word.
Your line: a clean corner. The prayer, step by step, starts here. See you tomorrow.
